notes.h: Effect of developing technology on industry (Higher Level only)
notes.b: New technology changes how work is organised, how many workers are needed and which skills are in demand.
points: Automation: machines and robots take over repetitive production and processing tasks, so fewer workers are needed for the same output.
Increased output with fewer workers reduces working hours in some industries and removes jobs at the lower-skilled end.
Computers and electronic communication change office work, creating new skilled jobs to design, install, maintain and operate technology.
Electronic communication allows home working but makes it harder to switch off, and reduces face-to-face social contact at work.
Technology also makes work safer and cleaner in some settings, as dangerous and dirty tasks are carried out by machines.

notes.h: Decline of primary and secondary industry and growth of services (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Employment has moved from extracting and manufacturing towards services.
points: Primary industry extracts resources: agriculture, fishing, forestry and mining.
Secondary industry manufactures and processes primary raw materials into finished goods.
Tertiary (service) industry provides services such as tourism, leisure, healthcare, transport, media, retail and education.
Automation reduced the number of manufacturing jobs, while service industries expanded and absorbed many workers.
Companies relocated production to lower-cost countries, causing job losses in manufacturing in Ireland.
Setting: compare Ireland's current occupational structure with that of fifty years ago, noting the shift from manual to service and professional work.

notes.b: As jobs have shifted towards services and technology, employers increasingly expect higher qualifications.
points: Service and technology jobs need literacy, numeracy, computing and communication skills, which are developed through education.
Employers use qualifications to select between applicants, so a larger share of applicants now hold them.
Early school leavers find it difficult to acquire work, as many jobs require a minimum level of education.
Continuing education, such as evening courses, distance learning and upskilling programmes, allows adults to gain qualifications and keep pace with technology.
Reskilling allows workers whose jobs have disappeared to move into new occupations.

notes.h: Increased participation by women (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Women's participation in paid employment has grown, with social and economic causes.
points: Women are better educated than in the past, and qualifications open access to professional and skilled work.
Income from paid work gives women financial independence and a stronger personal identity.
The growth of service industries created many jobs that suited women's skills and flexible hours.
Rising living costs and the need for a second income encourage women into paid employment.
Flexible hours and job-sharing make it possible to combine paid work with home and family responsibilities.
Better pay, pension entitlement and holiday arrangements make paid work more attractive.
Statutory protections for workers cover health and safety, pay and working time.
Safer and cleaner workplaces, made possible by technology, reduce risk of injury and illness.
Parental leave and career breaks allow workers to take time away for family reasons and return to their job.
Improved conditions have enabled many women to return to the workforce after raising children.

notes.h: Increasing flexibility in working hours (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Working time is now arranged in many ways other than the traditional full-time, fixed-hours week.
points: Flexitime: employees choose their start and finish times within agreed core hours.
Job-sharing: two people share one full-time post, dividing the hours and pay between them.
Part-time and term-time working: reduced hours, or work arranged around school terms.
Compressed or reduced working weeks, such as working longer days across fewer days.
Teleworking: working from home or another remote location using electronic communication.
Parental leave: unpaid leave for parents, taken in one block or spread over an agreed period until the child reaches a set age.
Career breaks: an agreed period of unpaid leave, after which the worker returns to their job.

notes.h: Effects of changing patterns of work (Higher Level only)
points: Workers displaced from manufacturing may need retraining before they can find work in services.
Flexible working helps parents plan childcare and family life more smoothly.
Blurred boundaries between work and home can increase stress and make it harder to switch off.
Families in which both parents work gain income but may face role overload and role conflict.
Employers gain access to a wider, more skilled labour pool and can keep staff by offering flexible arrangements.

keyTerms.definition: The use of machines or robots to carry out tasks previously done by people, reducing the number of workers needed.
Industry that extracts natural resources, such as agriculture, fishing, forestry and mining.
Industry that manufactures or processes primary raw materials into finished goods.
Industry that provides services, such as tourism, healthcare, transport, media and education.
The distribution of employment across types of occupation, such as manual, service and professional work.
A working arrangement in which employees choose their start and finish times within agreed core hours.
An arrangement in which two people share the hours and pay of one full-time post.
Working from home or another remote location, using electronic communication to stay connected with the employer.
Training workers in new skills so they can move into different occupations.
Unpaid leave that parents can take to care for a child, in one block or spread over an agreed period.

factCards.definition: Primary: extraction of resources such as farming, fishing, forestry and mining. Secondary: manufacturing and processing of raw materials into goods. Tertiary: services such as tourism, healthcare, transport, media and education.
Flexitime, where workers choose start and finish times within core hours; job-sharing, where two people share one post; part-time or term-time working; teleworking from home or a remote location.

factCards.term: Three effects of developing technology on work
factCards.definition: Automation reduces the number of workers needed for repetitive tasks; new skilled jobs are created to design and maintain technology; electronic communication blurs the boundary between work and home.

factCards.term: Two reasons for increased educational requirements
factCards.definition: Service and technology jobs need higher skills, and employers use qualifications to select between a growing number of qualified applicants.

factCards.term: Four reasons for increased participation by women
factCards.definition: Better education; financial independence; flexible hours and part-time work; the need for a second income to meet living costs.

factCards.term: Two ways flexible hours help working parents
factCards.definition: They allow parents to plan childcare around work schedules; they let parents spend more time with children, such as through a reduced working week.

questions.prompt: Describe two ways in which the decline of primary and secondary industry has changed employment in Ireland.
questions.model: Manufacturing jobs were lost as automation reduced the number of workers needed, and some companies relocated production to lower-cost countries. Employment grew instead in tertiary (service) industries such as tourism, healthcare, transport and education.

questions.prompt: Analyse how the growth of service industries and the increased participation of women have together changed the structure of the workforce. Give examples of the working arrangements that have supported this change.
questions.model: Service industries grew as manufacturing and primary industries declined, creating many jobs in tourism, healthcare, retail, transport and education. These jobs often suited the skills and flexible hours that many women wanted, so women's participation rose. Women's participation was supported by better education, increased need for a second income, and improved working conditions. Working arrangements supporting this change include flexitime, job-sharing, part-time and term-time working, teleworking and parental leave. Increased participation changed the workforce by raising the number of families in which both parents work and increasing demand for childcare.
